entries.summary: From the milestone release of Nomad 2.0 to the latest Nomad 2.1 capabilities, a look at how engineering advancements across Core Platform, Drivers, Autoscaler, and Terraform empower modern infrastructure teams.
entries.text: The future of orchestration is heterogeneous. Platform teams should not have to choose between containers, raw binaries, and virtual machines, or maintain separate, siloed control planes for each. Today’s infrastructure demands an orchestration platform that pairs high-throughput scheduling with granular kernel-level security and clean operational automation across them. This year, engineering across the Nomad ecosystem has focused on advancing that foundation. Spanning the Nomad 2.0 and 2.1 release cycles, from core consensus and performance enhancements to new scheduling governance, runtime drivers, autoscaling, and Terraform tooling, Nomad continues to evolve to meet the demands of modern production environments. Improve control plane performance and recovery Nomad 2.0 lets operators migrate the Raft log store from BoltDB to a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) backend, which offers better performance for write-heavy workloads. Nomad 2.0.5 added the plan_apply_pipeline setting, which lets operators control how many outstanding plans the leader allows when evaluating plans. For recovery, Nomad 2.1 adds nomad operator snapshot filter. It removes selected entries from a snapshot and writes the result to a copy. Operators can use it to clean up a snapshot before restoring it, or to remove a large number of pending evaluations when recovering a cluster from an outage. entries.title: Nomad in 2026: A Year of Scale, Security, and Ecosystem Velocity

entries.summary: As AI goes cloud native, learn how HashiCorp Vault helps secure Kubernetes data, workload trust, certificates, and application credentials.
entries.text: AI is moving beyond experimentation and into production, but security controls aren’t necessarily keeping pace. Recent IBM research shows 48% of surveyed executives say their organizations lack adequate protection for model inference and live AI usage, while 56% say the same about AI development and training. As organizations move AI applications, models, and autonomous agents into production environments orchestrated by platforms such as Kubernetes, closing that security gap requires looking beyond the AI model itself. This shift is reflected in team priorities and thought leadership, including the agenda at this year’s KubeCon. Moving a model from demo to production introduces challenges across compute, GPU utilization, model serving, networking, storage, observability, cost and most importantly, security. Autonomous AI agents add the consideration: how can workloads safely and securely interact with infrastructure, APIs, tools, and data. For platform and security teams, that changes the conversation. Securing AI on Kubernetes isn't only about protecting a model or application. It requires securing the infrastructure underneath it, including the data stored by Kubernetes, the identities and certificates workloads use to establish trust, and the credentials applications need to access other systems. Protect the Kubernetes foundation beneath AI workloads Kubernetes uses etcd as its backing store for cluster data, which can include Kubernetes Secrets and other sensitive config
entries.title: Building a secure foundation for AI on Kubernetes with HashiCorp Vault

entries.summary: Learn how Vault Radar and Vault help organizations find exposed secrets, improve remediation, and reduce credential risk across the application lifecycle.
entries.text: A recent software supply chain attack affecting tens of thousands of GitHub repositories highlights a security problem that is easy to underestimate: a credential does not stop being exposed simply because it has been deleted from the latest version of the code. Researchers uncovered a campaign in which attackers inserted a malicious GitHub Actions workflow into repositories they had permission to modify. Designed to look like a routine security audit, the workflow instead searched for and exfiltrated credentials. It targeted secrets available to GitHub Actions, but also searched repository files and complete Git history for credentials associated with cloud providers and AI services. That meant credentials developers had previously committed and later removed could still be discovered. The incident is another reminder that responding to exposed credentials requires more than cleaning up source code. Organizations need to understand where credentials have been exposed, remediate those credentials and ultimately improve how they are managed. HCP Vault Radar and HashiCorp Vault can help teams address different parts of that lifecycle, moving from discovering exposed secrets to bringing credentials under centralized management. A deleted secret can still be an exposed secret Accidentally committing a credential is not an unusual scenario in software development. entries.title: From exposed secrets to managed credentials: Reducing credential risk across the application lifecycle

entries.summary: Learn how Terraform and IBM Concert connect trusted infrastructure context, policy-driven governance, and vulnerability management to improve risk posture across the infrastructure lifecycle.
entries.text: Advances in AI are accelerating vulnerability discovery, uncovering previously unknown weaknesses and complex attack paths. Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning marked a major shift in the vulnerability landscape, demonstrating how frontier AI can identify vulnerabilities that have persisted through traditional testing and expert review. As discovery becomes faster and more sophisticated, organizations will face an even greater volume of findings to assess and prioritize. But finding more vulnerabilities is only the first step. To meaningfully reduce risk, teams need a way to determine which vulnerabilities matter most and a repeatable way to take action to address them. For many organizations, that path from detection to resolution remains fragmented. Disconnected workflows, manual handoffs, and complex infrastructure environments make it difficult to understand what is affected, whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited, and what changes are needed to resolve it. Until teams can turn those insights into action, vulnerabilities remain unresolved and organizations remain exposed. Improving infrastructure risk posture requires connecting vulnerability intelligence with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act. entries.title: From insight to action: improving infrastructure risk posture with Terraform and Concert

entries.summary: Consul 2.1.0 helps organizations simplify application access, strengthen networking resilience and security, modernize the underlying connectivity stack, and extend trusted connectivity to emerging AI workloads.
entries.text: Applications are becoming more distributed, and the connections between them are becoming more complex. Platform teams must securely expose services, enforce consistent access policies, keep application traffic available when infrastructure components are disrupted, and meet increasingly demanding security requirements. At the same time, AI agents, tools, and inference models are creating a new class of machine-to-machine interactions that enterprises need to identify, connect, and govern. Consul 2.1.0 addresses both realities: improving the networking foundation customers depend on today while introducing new building blocks for governing emerging agentic workloads. Simplify and govern application access with an enhanced API Gateway As organizations expose more services, application teams need to manage different protocols, TLS certificates, service discovery, authorization policies, and backend health. Handling each concern independently can increase both application complexity and the operational burden on platform teams. Consul 2.1.0 expands API Gateway to centralize more of those responsibilities. The Consul API gateway now supports end-to-end HTTP/2 and gRPC, allowing these protocols to be maintained from client to backend rather than being downgraded on the upstream connection. entries.title: Consul 2.1.0: Advancing secure, resilient connectivity for modern and agentic applications

entries.summary: Use the Terraform policy agent to convert existing Sentinel and OPA policies into tested Terraform policies. Run it in a container with the model provider you choose.
entries.text: Your Sentinel and OPA policies represent years of work: security and compliance decisions, edge cases, and lessons learned, all captured as code. As infrastructure has evolved, governance increasingly depends on how resources relate, on external context, and on the full infrastructure lifecycle. With the general availability of Terraform policy, a declarative, HCL-based policy as code framework integrated with Terraform, teams can enforce governance in the same language and workflows they already use to manage infrastructure. The hard part is getting there. Converting policies manually means re-reading their logic, mapping it to Terraform resources and attributes, and writing and testing new policies across an entire library. Today, we are announcing the general availability of the Terraform policy agent, which converts existing Sentinel and Open Policy Agent (OPA) policies into Terraform policies. For each policy, it generates a policy file, tests, and reports describing the conversion and any limitations. It runs as a container from Docker Hub, and you choose the model provider: GitHub Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, or LiteLLM. Why bring your policies to Terraform policy Terraform policy builds on what Sentinel and OPA started, bringing policy closer to the infrastructure it governs. entries.title: Migrate Sentinel and OPA policies to Terraform policy faster with the Terraform policy agent

entries.summary: AI credentials can easily spread across development workflows. Learn how Vault Radar and Vault help teams find, remediate, and securely manage them.
entries.text: AI development may be changing how applications are built, but many of the security problems underneath them are familiar. Applications need credentials to connect to models, cloud services, databases, development tools, and other systems. As teams experiment with new AI services and move applications toward production, those credentials can spread across repositories and development workflows just as other secrets do. An API key gets added to a configuration file to get a prototype running. A developer uses it during testing. The application evolves, the team moves on, but the credential remains. Now the organization has two problems: How do you find credentials that have ended up where they shouldn't be, and once you find them, how do you keep them from ending up there again? That is where secret discovery and secrets management need to come together. AI adds another dimension to secrets sprawl The problem starts well before a credential is compromised. A credential that lives outside an organization's secrets management practices can be difficult to inventory, monitor, and remediate. And simply searching today's code isn't necessarily enough. Credentials can persist in Git history even after they have been removed from the latest version of a file. AI applications often depend on model providers, cloud infrastructure, vector databases, and developer tooling, all of which introduce additional credentials that need to be managed securely. entries.text: Terraform has long helped platform teams standardize how infrastructure is provisioned and managed. As Terraform adoption grows across an organization, the next challenge is making that infrastructure easier for developers to consume. Developers shouldn't need to understand every Terraform module, workspace, or organizational standard before they can get the infrastructure they need. At the same time, platform teams need to maintain control over what gets provisioned and how. We're investing in making self-service a native part of the Terraform experience. That means giving developers a simpler way to discover and consume approved infrastructure, while giving platform teams the controls they need to define and govern those experiences. Increasingly, it also means making that same self-service foundation available to AI agents. Terraform Developer Portal: a native self-service experience for developers Terraform Developer Portal (TDP), provides a native self-service experience for developers to discover, provision, and manage infrastructure through Terraform. Platform teams can expose existing Terraform modules as curated Templates, defining the inputs developers need to provide while maintaining control over how infrastructure is provisioned. For example, a platform team might expose an approved AWS module as a Template such as Create an Application Service. entries.summary: HashiCorp Secure Hub enters public preview, delivering centralized visibility, reporting, and governance across Vault environments at enterprise scale.
entries.text: HashiCorp Vault has become a critical security platform for organizations managing secrets, credentials, certificates, cryptographic services, and machine and agentic access across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. As adoption expands to more applications, teams, business units, and regions, however, organizations face a new challenge: understanding and governing their growing Vault estate as a whole. What can be managed effectively within individual environments becomes increasingly complex as organizations need to understand operational health, security resources, usage, and lifecycle activity at enterprise scale. Today, we are announcing the public preview of HashiCorp Secure Hub, a common governance layer that gives organizations a unified way to understand and govern their Vault estate. Secure Hub brings together visibility, reporting, and operational context from distributed Vault environments, giving platform, security, and governance teams a more complete view of the security resources they manage. Secure Hub complements the security controls and enforcement within Vault Enterprise rather than replacing them. Vault continues to secure and enforce access within individual environments, while Secure Hub provides the enterprise-wide context needed to govern the broader Vault estate. entries.text: Enterprises rely on HashiCorp Vault to secure access to sensitive systems, applications, and data across increasingly complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments. But the environment around those applications is changing. Machine identities continue to grow, certificate lifecycles are becoming shorter, cryptographic requirements are evolving, and AI agents are creating a new class of autonomous workload that must be identified, authorized, and governed. Today, we are announcing the public preview of Vault Arc, expanding the Vault portfolio with new capabilities designed for these emerging security and operational requirements. Vault Arc is still Vault. It builds on the role Vault plays in enterprise security while introducing a new approach to how security resources are modeled, governed, queried, and operated. Importantly, Vault Arc complements Vault Enterprise rather than requiring customers to replace it. Organizations can continue deploying and expanding Vault Enterprise for existing and new workloads while evaluating Vault Arc where its capabilities provide additional value. Extending Vault for what's next Modernization isn't simply about replacing existing technology. It's about giving organizations the flexibility to respond as their infrastructure, workloads, and security requirements change. At TechXchange, IBM is introducing new capabilities across Verify, Vault, and Boundary to help enterprises establish trusted identities, enforce appropriate access, strengthen cryptographic security, and govern activity across hybrid environments, creating a stronger foundation for agentic AI and autonomous operations. Agent Identity enables trusted AI agents across the enterprise AI agents are rapidly becoming active participants in enterprise operations. As agents gain the ability to access systems, invoke tools, orchestrate workflows, and act on behalf of users, organizations need a consistent way to establish agent identity, manage delegated authority, enforce access controls, and maintain accountability throughout the agent lifecycle. Traditional identity systems were not designed to address these new requirements. IBM Agent Identity, now generally available, helps organizations secure AI agents as first-class identities through a coordinated identity control plane. entries.summary: Boundary 1.1 improves integration with app tokens, simplifies cross-account AWS host discovery, and introduces an MCP server.
entries.text: Boundary 1.1 is now available with administrative improvements for enterprise scale and simpler external app integration. A new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server will also be available in public preview that allows administrators and end users to interact with Boundary using natural language through AI-driven interfaces. App Tokens This release introduces app tokens, which are used to securely integrate external tools with scoped access to Boundary. Prior to this release, when an external machine or application needed access to Boundary for CI/CD workflows, infrastructure automation, observability, or any type of integration, it relied on a shared human credential or an admin-managed static password, which posed a security concern as password accounts are long lived and never expire. In addition, when human password credentials were used, the authorization tokens given to external applications were short-lived and valid for only seven days. This means applications would only be able to perform API calls to Boundary for seven days before the application needed to re-authenticate and request a new token. This was an inefficient process that was brittle and not very secure. App tokens now allow administrators to provision tokens with fine-grained permissions for machine-to-machine communication with Boundary. entries.text: Infrastructure automation has transformed how organizations provision and manage infrastructure. But as agents begin to participate alongside humans in infrastructure operations, automation alone is no longer enough. The next challenge is autonomy: How do we give agents the ability to act safely within guardrails? Answering that question requires more than giving agents access to infrastructure. They need trusted context to understand the environment and the potential impact of change, governed workflows to translate decisions into action, and continuous governance to maintain trust and control as infrastructure evolves. Three fundamental barriers stand in the way. Lack of Trusted Infrastructure Context Many organizations have adopted Infrastructure as Code to standardize provisioning and improve consistency across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. However, as infrastructure environments grow in scale and complexity, and agents begin participating in infrastructure workflows, provisioning alone is no longer sufficient. Organizations need a trusted understanding of their infrastructure estate to make informed decisions. Most organizations lack a complete and trusted view of their infrastructure, including resource relationships, dependencies, governance posture, compliance status, and operational context. entries.summary: Vault 2.2 introduces TPM Support so on-prem applications can authenticate using a virtual TPM, reducing bootstrap credential distribution and the risk of credential reuse from another machine.
entries.text: Your application starts on a virtual machine. Its database password is safely stored in Vault. Access policies are in place. Everything is ready—except the application needs a credential before Vault will let it retrieve anything. Someone has to get that first credential to the right machine. Then protect it, limit its use, and replace it when necessary. Repeat that across a fleet, and the first connection becomes a security risk of its own. This is the Secret Zero problem. And for teams running applications on on-premise VMs, it can stand between adopting centralized secrets management and relying on yet another system to distribute secrets. Vault 2.2 introduces TPM Support for Vault Enterprise. Linux VMs can authenticate using keys bound to an enrolled virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM), removing the need to deliver a reusable bootstrap secret to each VM for this authentication flow. For platform teams, that means a new way to establish trust in the applications running on infrastructure they already operate. For security teams, it means stronger protection against credentials being copied from one machine and reused on another. Bring infrastructure-based authentication to on-prem VMs Cloud identity services give workloads a way to authenticate without teams distributing their own bootstrap secrets. entries.title: Eliminate Secret Zero for on-prem workloads with Vault 2.2
